title: Hiring freeze policy for high interest rates
description: Decide which roles to keep, gate behind milestones or pause while rates are high, then lift the freeze in stages.
boardSummary: Keep roles that protect reliability, renewals and cash visibility open. Review each role’s cash impact within two quarters.
Approve unproven expansion hires one at a time against a 30-day milestone. Pause roles with no measurable business case.
Review the hiring policy when cash conversion worsens for 30 days, sales cycles lengthen and near-term financing becomes less likely.
Reopen hiring in stages after two consecutive monthly readings show stable burn multiple and demand quality.

sections.heading: Review roles before freezing hiring
paragraphs: A hire commits cash to payroll and onboarding. Compare the cost of leaving a role unfilled with the cost and time needed to unwind it if demand falls.
Replacing a reliability bottleneck and staffing an unproven growth team carry different risks. Review them separately before imposing a blanket freeze.

sections.heading: Which roles to approve or pause
paragraphs: SAFE roles protect current operations or revenue: production reliability, renewals support and finance controls for cash visibility. Keep them open with constrained approval.
RISKY roles support initiatives that have not shown repeatable demand. Approve one hire, set a 30-day evidence target and review the result before approving another.
DANGEROUS roles lack a clear owner, a validated market or measurable milestones. Pause them until the business case and resume conditions are explicit.

sections.heading: When to resume hiring
paragraphs: Set resume conditions using burn multiple, pipeline conversion and cash remaining after committed spend. Review demand and delivery weekly; use monthly readings to decide whether to reopen hiring.
An example requires three conditions: stable win rates and churn for 30 days, shorter delivery cycles with fewer emergency escalations, and financing access that no longer requires immediate cuts.
When all three hold, reopen one or two SAFE hiring groups first. Keep RISKY hires tied to milestones and DANGEROUS roles paused until two monthly confirmations pass.

sections.heading: Build the role list
paragraphs: List each open role and planned backfill with its purpose, cost if unfilled, evidence window and time to reverse. Classify it as SAFE, RISKY or DANGEROUS.

Review the list with finance and hiring managers. Record one measurable indicator per approval, the pause and resume lines, and an owner and review date for each exception. Include the list in the weekly memo.

faqs.question: Should startups freeze hiring when rates are high?
faqs.answer: High rates alone do not require a blanket freeze. Keep roles that protect operations or current revenue open, tie expansion hires to milestones and pause roles without a measurable business case.

faqs.question: How long should a hiring freeze last in a tightening market?
faqs.answer: Review monthly. Reopen in stages after two consecutive monthly readings show stable burn multiple and demand quality; keep the role-specific milestones in place.

faqs.question: What should I send my board about hiring?
faqs.answer: Send the approved role list, exceptions with owners and review dates, and the pause and resume lines.

title: How much runway should a startup have?
description: Use 18–24 months as a planning range in a tightening market, then adjust for the time it takes to cut costs or raise money.
keyword: how much runway should a startup have
boardSummary: Use 18–24 months as a planning range during tightening. Favor the upper end when commitments are slow to reverse or financing is uncertain.
Separate the cash floor for essential operations from the buffer available for new investments.
Release new spending in stages after demand and financing access improve for 30 days. Keep projected runway above the agreed floor.

sections.heading: Account for the time needed to cut costs
paragraphs: Set the target using demand uncertainty, fixed costs and the time needed to respond when assumptions fail. A payroll or vendor commitment may keep consuming cash for months after you decide to stop.
Separate the cash needed to sustain essential operations without emergency financing from the buffer available for new investments. Model both before approving more spending.

sections.heading: Runway bands
paragraphs: SAFE band: 20–24 months when financing is uncertain and a large share of costs is hard to reverse.
RISKY band: 15–19 months with mixed demand. Review burn multiple monthly, set stop conditions for each investment and hold irreversible expansion.
DANGEROUS band: below 15 months with limited financing options or high fixed costs. Inventory commitments, sequence cash-preservation actions and freeze non-core spending.
These are planning defaults. Adjust them for revenue concentration, collection risk and the time your company needs to cut costs.

sections.heading: When to change the runway target
paragraphs: Agree on numerical limits and review periods for retention, gross margin and cash forecast error before changing the runway target.
Example pause line: retention stays below your limit for two consecutive monthly readings while gross margin keeps falling. Increase the runway target and suspend non-core commitments.

Example resume line: renewals and conversion improve for 30 days, cash forecast error narrows and financing access improves. Release one investment installment while keeping projected runway above the agreed floor.

sections.heading: Test the cash forecast
paragraphs: Calculate runway under a base case, a downside case and a case where payroll and vendor costs take longer to unwind. List each major cost with its exit terms and time to stop.

Check the roadmap against those cases. Fund retention and measurable customer learning before scaling new initiatives. Seek board approval for any plan that would take projected runway below the agreed floor.

faqs.question: What runway target should startups use in a recession risk environment?
faqs.answer: Start with an 18–24 month planning range during tightening. Adjust it for fixed costs, collection risk and financing access.

faqs.question: Is 12 months of runway enough in a tightening market?
faqs.answer: Test whether cash lasts through a downside case and the time needed to cut costs. A 12-month runway leaves less room for delays; reversible costs and available financing matter.

faqs.question: How do boards evaluate runway confidence?
faqs.answer: Compare downside cash forecasts, recent forecast errors and the time needed to exit major commitments.
